Description

At sites where the cell holds on to the extracellular matrix, the focal adhesion protein paxillin assembles its own ERK cascade. After stimulation with hepatocyte growth factor, paxillin phosphorylated on tyrosine binds inactive ERK, and paxillin also binds RAF and MEK, forming a complex that activates ERK in place [1]. Active ERK then phosphorylates paxillin on Ser83, which lets paxillin bind focal adhesion kinase (FAK). FAK, now active at the adhesion, recruits phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and activates Rac, which drives cell spreading [2]. ERK phosphorylation of paxillin serines is also needed for growth signals in prostate cancer cells [3]. The adaptor GIT1, which binds MEK1, recruits ERK to focal adhesions and is needed for its activation there [4].

References

  2. Ishibe S, Joly D, Liu ZX, Cantley LG. Paxillin serves as an ERK-regulated scaffold for coordinating FAK and Rac activation in epithelial morphogenesis. Mol Cell. 2004;16(2):257-67. PMID: 15494312. doi: 10.1016/j.molcel.2004.10.006.
  3. Sen A, O'Malley K, Wang Z, Raj GV, Defranco DB, Hammes SR. Paxillin regulates androgen- and epidermal growth factor-induced MAPK signaling and cell proliferation in prostate cancer cells. J Biol Chem. 2010;285(37):28787-95. PMID: 20628053. doi: 10.1074/jbc.M110.134064.
  4. Yin G, Zheng Q, Yan C, Berk BC. GIT1 is a scaffold for ERK1/2 activation in focal adhesions. J Biol Chem. 2005;280(30):27705-12. PMID: 15923189. doi: 10.1074/jbc.M502271200.
